summary: Defines how audio compressed with the open-source Speex voice codec is packed into RTP packets for sending over the network, such as in VoIP calls. It also describes the parameters needed to describe Speex streams in SDP, the format used to set up media sessions.

eli5.summary: Speex squeezes voice into small pieces. This explains how to put those pieces into envelopes, called packets, and how to write the address label so the other side knows how to open them.

subtitle: How Speex-compressed voice is packed into RTP packets and described in SDP for VoIP calls.

tldr.problem: Speex is an open-source voice codec, but VoIP software needs an agreed way to put its bit stream into RTP packets and to announce its settings during session setup.
tldr.mechanism: The payload is just the Speex encoder's bits, one or more 20 msec frames per packet, padded to an octet boundary, with no extra header. The audio/speex media type and its SDP mapping carry rate, mode, vbr and cng settings.
tldr.outcome: Any Speex sender and receiver can interoperate in RTP, because each frame carries its own sampling rate and mode, so the decoder needs no out-of-band information.

today: RFC 5574 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the document that defines the RTP payload format and SDP usage for Speex.

sections.title: The Speex Codec and Compliance
sections.content:
Speex is an open-source voice codec for VoIP. It is based on Code Excited Linear Prediction (CELP) and supports narrowband (nominal 8 kHz), wideband (nominal 16 kHz) and ultra-wideband (nominal 32 kHz). Its listed characteristics include integrated wideband and narrowband in one bit stream, dynamic bit-rate switching, variable bit-rate (VBR), voice activity detection (VAD) and variable complexity.

Bit-rates range from 2.15 kbit/s to 44 kbit/s. An implementation that cannot support everything MUST at least support narrowband (8 kHz) at 8 kbit/s, which is narrowband mode 3. Narrowband at 15 kbit/s (mode 5) and wideband at 27.8 kbit/s (wideband mode 8) are RECOMMENDED. The sampling rate MUST be 8, 16 or 32 kHz, and only single-channel (mono) audio is defined.
sections.eli5: Speex is a free way to shrink talking into very little data. The RFC says the bare minimum every Speex program must understand, so two programs can always at least talk.

sections.title: RTP Header Use and Payload Layout
sections.content:
The payload format adds no header of its own. The standard RTP header from RFC 3550 is followed by one or more Speex frames, and an optional padding terminator.

  • Payload type: assigned by the RTP profile in use or signaled dynamically, for example through SDP. It is out of scope here.
  • Marker (M) bit: set to one on the first packet sent after a silence period during which packets were not sent contiguously.
  • Extension (X) bit: defined by the RTP profile.
  • Timestamp: a 32-bit word for the sampling instant of the first frame in the packet.
sections.eli5: A voice packet is the normal RTP envelope with the voice pieces dropped straight inside. The envelope gets a special mark on the first packet after a quiet stretch.

sections.title: Speex Frames, Padding and Packing
sections.content:
Packetizing only needs the bit sequence produced by the Speex encoder, which the receiver gives unchanged to the decoder. A typical frame at the maximum bit-rate is about 110 octets. The total size SHOULD stay below the path MTU, and frames MUST NOT be fragmented across RTP packets. Frames go in oldest first, in consecutive time order.

A packet MAY mix frames of the same or different bit-rates, because each frame carries its sampling rate (narrowband, wideband or ultra-wideband) and mode (bit-rate) in-band. The encoder can change bit-rate at any 20 msec frame boundary and the decoder needs no separate notice. The decoder also finds the 20 msec boundaries between frames.

The payload MUST be padded to a whole number of octets. The padding bits are LSB-aligned and consist of a 0 followed by all ones to the end of the octet. This applies only to the last frame in the packet. The RFC's example shows a single frame with 5 bits of padding.
sections.eli5: The voice pieces go in the envelope oldest first. Each piece says how fancy it is, so the listener never needs a note from the sender. If a piece ends mid-byte, filler bits top it up.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type audio/speex. The required parameter rate is the RTP clock rate, which equals the sampling rate and MUST be 8000, 16000 or 32000. Optional parameters:

  • ptime and maxptime SHOULD be multiples of 20 msec.
  • vbr is on, off or vad, defaulting to off. With vad, constant bit-rate is used but silence is encoded as special short frames.
  • cng is on or off, defaulting to off, and controls whether silence frames carry comfort noise.
  • mode is a quoted, comma-separated list of decoding modes in order of preference. Valid values are 1 to 8 or any for narrowband, and 0 to 10 or any for wideband and ultra-wideband. If omitted it equals mode="3,any" for narrowband and mode="8,any" otherwise.

The vbr, cng and mode values are preferences to the encoder. Listing modes also implies the implementation can encode them. An application MUST be able to decode any Speex frame unless the SDP clearly says some modes are unsupported, for example by leaving out mode="any".

In SDP, the type audio goes on the m= line and speex plus the rate go in a=rtpmap. ptime and maxptime become their own attributes, and the rest go in a=fmtp as semicolon-separated pairs. Offer and answer parameters are completely orthogonal. The media type depends on RTP framing and is not defined for other framing protocols.
sections.eli5: This is the label on the envelope. It says how fast the voice was recorded and what quality you would like back, and it lists which qualities you can read.

sections.title: SDP Examples and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC gives SDP examples. One offer prefers mode 4 at 8000 Hz and adds any to say all modes are decodable, since the remote party might still send others. Another lists only modes 3 and 5, so the remote party MUST NOT use any other mode. Others show vbr=on;cng=on, vbr=vad, and two sampling rates in one offer (16000 Hz mode 10 or 8000 Hz mode 7).

For packetization time, Speex uses 20 msec frames, so a ptime of 40 means two frames per packet. A ptime that is not a multiple of 20 is rounded up internally, so 30 becomes 40. Care is needed so the RTP packet does not exceed the path MTU.

Implementers should note that each frame holds everything needed to decode itself. The mode and ptime values in SDP MUST NOT be used for decoding.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample labels, such as 'please send me my favorite quality' or 'I can only read these two qualities.' Even then, the pieces tell the reader how to open them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets using this format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and any RTP profile. Confidentiality comes from encryption, and because compression is applied end-to-end, encryption can be done after compression with no conflict.

The RFC notes a possible denial-of-service threat for encodings with non-uniform receiver-end computational load, where an attacker injects datagrams that are costly to decode. It states that this encoding does not show any significant non-uniformity. As with any IP protocol, a receiver can still be overloaded by too many packets. Network-layer authentication may discard unwanted sources, though its own processing cost may be too high.
sections.eli5: Speex packets are no easier to trick than any other voice packets. A flood of mail can still bury the mailbox, but no single Speex piece is extra hard to open.
